implementation_notes: JavaScript answers the many-optional-parameters problem with one object argument: destructuring with defaults in the parameter list, or a { ...DEFAULTS, ...overrides } merge, names each setting at the call site, keeps defaults in a single place and makes "the same configuration with one change" a one-liner. The classic fluent builder survives where the object is grown from conditional steps - Knex's query builder and similar SQL/ORM builders chain clauses and only execute at the end - so reach for it when construction is incremental rather than a fixed set of options.
pitfalls: Destructuring defaults apply only to undefined: a null (a common JSON-parsing result) overwrites the default and fails later, far from the call site.
A shallow spread replaces a whole nested object, so spreading a nested config alone drops every default inside it; nested settings have to be merged explicitly.
Nothing validates the keys: a typo in an options object is accepted and ignored, because plain objects have no schema.

variants.name: Fluent chain (query and DSL builders)
variants.idiom_name: class with methods returning this plus a terminal build()/execute()
variants.implementation_notes: For incremental construction the fluent chain is still the JavaScript norm: each method mutates the accumulated state and returns this (or, in a closure-based builder, the builder object, because arrow functions have no this), and a terminal method serialises, validates and freezes the result - Knex's query builder is the canonical example. The idiom's weakness is mutability: Knex documents that most methods mutate and return the same object, so branching from a stored builder requires .clone().
pitfalls: Mutating chains alias: two branches taken from one builder stack each other's clauses unless the builder is immutable or explicitly cloned (Knex's .clone()).
Arrow functions capture the enclosing this, so returning this from them returns the wrong object; a closure-based builder must return the builder reference explicitly.
Type inference collapses over a mutable fluent API: the chain has one type, so a step that should narrow the result has to be assigned to a new variable.
